## Learning objectives {#jmetrics-objectives}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

- Explain the citation windows and data requirements of JIF, CiteScore and SNIP
- Explain why network-based journal metrics differ from simple citation ratios
- Summarise current cumulative citations and recorded references in journal cohorts
- Distinguish those descriptive summaries from official journal metrics
- Evaluate journals using appropriate evidence rather than a single number

## Setup {#jmetrics-setup}

```{r}
#| label: 11-setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openalexR)
library(glue)
library(gt)

set.seed(20260509)

source(here::here("R", "api_helpers.R"))
source(here::here("R", "utils.R"))
source(here::here("R", "sci_palette.R"))
```

## Conceptual background {#jmetrics-background}

Journal-level metrics summarise particular aspects of a journal's citation
record. The two-year **Journal Impact Factor** (JIF) for year *t* counts citations
received in year *t* to the journal's content from years *t*-1 and *t*-2, divided
by its citable items from those two publication years. The numerator can include
citations to document types excluded from the denominator. The citation year,
publication cohort and document-type rules are distinct parts of the definition;
see [Clarivate's calculation explanation](https://clarivate.libguides.com/jcr/).

**CiteScore** uses a four-year publication window and counts citations received
within that same four-year interval. Its eligible document types include articles,
reviews, conference papers, book chapters and data papers in both the numerator
and denominator; it does not simply include every document type. See
[Elsevier's metric definitions](https://www.elsevier.com/en-gb/researcher/author/tools-and-resources/measuring-a-journals-impact).

**SNIP** (Source-Normalized Impact per Paper) adjusts for citation practices using
information from the *citing* side, with specified reference and weighting rules.
It is not a journal's citation average divided by the median reference count in
its own papers. The revised method is described by
[Waltman et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2012.11.011).
**SJR** (SCImago Journal Rank) and **Eigenfactor** use citation networks to weight
citations according to their source; a simple citation count does not reproduce
those network calculations [@waltman2016].

The published indicators use specified database coverage, document eligibility,
time windows and methods. An alternative calculation needs its own explicit
definition and validation [@visser2021]. The OpenAlex example below computes
current cumulative citation and recorded-reference summaries only. It neither
implements nor estimates JIF, CiteScore, SNIP, SJR or Eigenfactor.

DORA [@dora2012] warns against using a journal metric as a measure of an individual
article's quality. Journal averages cannot establish the quality of a particular
paper, and citation distributions within journals can be highly uneven [@hicks2015].

## Worked example {#jmetrics-example}

### Selecting journals

We use five journals in information science and research evaluation. Source
identities were checked against OpenAlex on 30 October 2026. The JASIST record
below is the current *Journal of the Association for Information Science and
Technology*, appropriate to the 2021–2022 publication cohort; historical titles
can have separate source records.

```{r}
#| label: 11-define-journals
journals <- tribble(
  ~short_name,        ~source_id,
  "Scientometrics",   "S148561398",
  "J Informetrics",   "S205292342",
  "Quant Sci Stud",   "S4210195326",
  "JASIST",           "S4210197613",
  "Res Evaluation",   "S16793705"
)
```

### Fetching a publication cohort

Fetch records classified as articles and published in 2021–2022. Their
`cited_by_count` values are **cumulative citations at retrieval**, not citations
received in a specified historical year. The query restricts publication dates;
it does not restrict the dates on which citations were received. Results describe
the retrieved records and require coverage checks before being treated as complete
journal output.

```{r}
#| label: 11-fetch-journal-data
#| cache: true
fetch_journal_works <- function(source_id, from_year, to_year) {
  res <- fetch_openalex(
    entity = "works",
    primary_location.source.id = source_id,
    from_publication_date = paste0(from_year, "-01-01"),
    to_publication_date = paste0(to_year, "-12-31"),
    type = "article"
  )
  if (!is.data.frame(res) || !nrow(res)) {
    stop(glue("No usable records for {source_id}; check the query and provider response before comparing journals."))
  }
  res
}

journal_works <- journals |>
  mutate(data = map(source_id, \(sid) fetch_journal_works(sid, 2021, 2022)))
```

Provider errors propagate instead of being converted to zero publications or
citations. An empty result stops the worked comparison; it is not evidence that
a journal has no output.

### Cumulative citation summaries

The citation mean uses only observed citation counts, with that denominator
reported. Missing counts are not zero. A total over observed values is not a
complete journal total when records or counts are missing.

```{r}
#| label: 11-citation-summary
summarise_journal_records <- function(d) {
  required <- c("id", "cited_by_count", "referenced_works_count")
  if (!is.data.frame(d) || !nrow(d) || !all(required %in% names(d))) {
    stop("Journal summaries need nonempty records with IDs, citation counts and reference counts.")
  }
  if (anyNA(d$id) || any(!nzchar(d$id)) || anyDuplicated(d$id)) {
    stop("Journal work IDs must be present and unique.")
  }
  for (column in c("cited_by_count", "referenced_works_count")) {
    values <- d[[column]]
    if (!is.numeric(values) || any(!is.na(values) & (!is.finite(values) | values < 0))) {
      stop("Citation and reference counts must be finite nonnegative numbers or missing.")
    }
  }
  citations <- d$cited_by_count[!is.na(d$cited_by_count)]
  references <- d$referenced_works_count[!is.na(d$referenced_works_count)]
  tibble(
    n_articles = nrow(d), n_citations_observed = length(citations),
    observed_citation_sum = if (length(citations)) sum(citations) else NA_real_,
    mean_cumulative_citations = if (length(citations)) mean(citations) else NA_real_,
    median_cumulative_citations = if (length(citations)) median(citations) else NA_real_,
    n_references_observed = length(references),
    median_recorded_references = if (length(references)) median(references) else NA_real_
  )
}

journal_summary <- journal_works |>
  mutate(summary = map(data, summarise_journal_records)) |>
  unnest(summary) |>
  select(-data) |>
  arrange(short_name)

journal_summary |>
  select(short_name, n_articles, n_citations_observed, observed_citation_sum,
         mean_cumulative_citations, median_cumulative_citations) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean_cumulative_citations, median_cumulative_citations), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(short_name = "Journal", n_articles = "Retrieved articles (2021–22)",
             n_citations_observed = "Observed citation counts",
             observed_citation_sum = "Sum of observed cumulative citations",
             mean_cumulative_citations = "Mean cumulative citations",
             median_cumulative_citations = "Median cumulative citations")
```

### Recorded reference counts

`referenced_works_count` describes the references recorded for the fetched
journal articles. It is not the reference-list information for papers citing
those articles, and it need not capture every reference in the original texts.
We report it separately rather than dividing citations by it or calling it
citation potential.

```{r}
#| label: 11-reference-summary
journal_summary |>
  select(short_name, n_articles, n_references_observed, median_recorded_references) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(short_name = "Journal", n_articles = "Retrieved articles",
             n_references_observed = "Observed reference counts",
             median_recorded_references = "Median recorded references")
```

### Visualization

```{r}
#| label: 11-fig-jmetrics-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Current cumulative citations and recorded references for the retrieved 2021–2022 article cohorts, shown as separate descriptive quantities."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels show journal mean cumulative citations at retrieval and median recorded references in those same journal articles; neither panel is an official journal metric."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
combined <- journal_summary |>
  select(short_name, mean_cumulative_citations, median_recorded_references) |>
  pivot_longer(-short_name, names_to = "summary", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(summary = recode(summary,
    mean_cumulative_citations = "Mean cumulative citations",
    median_recorded_references = "Median recorded references"))

ggplot(combined, aes(x = value, y = short_name)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = palette_sci(1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ summary, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Descriptive value (see panel)", y = NULL) +
  theme_sci()
```

## Diagnostics and interpretation {#jmetrics-diagnostics}

- **Coverage**: Report source IDs, publication filters, retrieval dates and the number of retrieved records. Reconcile these with the intended corpus before interpreting output counts.
- **Missing data**: Compare the retrieved-record count with each observed denominator. An all-missing citation column produces missing summaries, not a zero-citation journal.
- **Time**: Older papers have had longer to accumulate citations. A publication-date filter cannot create an annual citation window from a current cumulative count.
- **Scope**: References in the journal's own articles describe those records; they do not supply the citing-side data needed for SNIP.
- **Comparisons**: Differences can reflect field mix, document classification, coverage and citation exposure. Agreement between descriptive rankings does not validate an official metric or justify an evaluation decision.

## Limitations and responsible use {#jmetrics-limitations}

<div class="callout callout-warn">
## Limitations and responsible use

- **Journal summaries are not article-quality measures.** Means can conceal skewed citation distributions and do not establish a particular paper's quality [@dora2012].
- **Targets can distort behaviour.** Citation stacking, coercive citation and denominator manipulation are risks when metrics become targets [@goodhart1984].
- **These are descriptive snapshots.** They are not JIF, CiteScore, SNIP or substitutes for those indicators. Reusing a familiar label does not supply the missing citation windows or methodology.
- **Field dependence and metadata coverage remain.** The example performs no field normalisation and cannot establish a fair ranking across disciplines [@waltman2016].
</div>

## Common pitfalls {#jmetrics-pitfalls}

<div class="callout callout-stop">
## Common pitfalls

- **Relabeling cumulative citations as annual citations.** JIF needs citations received in one specified year to the preceding two publication years.
- **Using the wrong side of a citation link.** The cited journal's own reference counts do not describe the reference lists of its citing works.
- **Treating absence as zero.** Failed requests, empty responses and missing values require explicit handling before computing a denominator.
- **Ranking journals by a single number.** Indicator definitions, distributions, coverage and disciplinary context matter alongside any numerical comparison.
</div>

## Exercises {#jmetrics-exercises}

1. **Cohort sensitivity.** Fetch 2019–2022 articles for one of the verified source IDs and compare their cumulative citation summary with the 2021–2022 cohort. Explain why widening the publication cohort does not compute CiteScore.

2. **Descriptive association.** Compute Spearman correlation between the journal means of cumulative citations and medians of recorded references, using complete pairs. Explain why any association does not validate SNIP or establish field normalisation.

3. **Missing-data denominator.** For three invented records with citation counts 0, 20 and missing, calculate the observed citation sum and mean using the helper. Compare that mean with dividing the observed sum by all three records. Also check a cohort whose citation counts are all missing.

4. **Self-citation design.** Specify the citation edges, citing-journal identities, time window and denominator needed to measure a journal self-citation share. Explain why the fetched cumulative counts and reference counts are insufficient.

## Further reading {#jmetrics-reading}

- @garfield1955 --- The original proposal for citation indexes.
- @waltman2016 --- Review of citation impact indicators and their data requirements.
- [Clarivate's JIF calculation](https://clarivate.libguides.com/jcr/) and [Elsevier's metric definitions](https://www.elsevier.com/en-gb/researcher/author/tools-and-resources/measuring-a-journals-impact) --- Provider definitions of citation windows and eligible documents.
- [Waltman et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2012.11.011) --- The revised SNIP methodology.
- @hicks2015; @dora2012 --- Responsible use of journal-level metrics.
- @visser2021 --- Database coverage differences.
- @priem2022 --- OpenAlex as an open bibliographic data source.
